blocks.markdown:
## What fenofibrate is

Fenofibrate is a **fibrate**, a family of medicines that mainly lower **triglycerides**, the fats the body stores and carries in the blood as fuel. It is one tablet a day, taken on top of diet, exercise and weight loss, not instead of them.

This module is built on one document: the **SmPC** (summary of product characteristics, the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers) of Secalip Supra 160 mg, authorised in Spain and held by Lacer, S.A. The version used is the text revised in December 2020. Where another source disagrees with it on what is approved, the SmPC wins.

## What it is approved for

The SmPC lists three uses, all alongside diet:

- Very high triglycerides (the label says *severe hypertriglyceridaemia*), with or without low **HDL cholesterol**, the fraction carried in particles that move cholesterol away from the arteries.
- **Mixed hyperlipidaemia**, meaning both cholesterol and triglycerides are raised, when a **statin** (the standard first cholesterol medicine) cannot be used or is not tolerated.
- Mixed hyperlipidaemia in people at high cardiovascular risk, added to a statin, when triglycerides and HDL cholesterol stay poorly controlled.

Notice what is missing: ordinary high cholesterol as a first treatment. That is deliberate, and Lesson 3 explains how it came about.

## What it does to blood fats

Across its clinical trials, the SmPC reports total cholesterol falling by 20–25%, triglycerides by 40–55%, and HDL cholesterol rising by 10–30%. In people with high cholesterol, **LDL cholesterol**, the fraction most closely tied to artery disease, fell by 20–35%.

Read those as orientation, not as results. The SmPC gives them as ranges without naming the **comparator** (what the medicine was compared against) or the time point. You need both before any number means something.

## What it does to heart attacks and strokes

The picture here is more modest than the lipid numbers suggest. The SmPC states that fibrates may reduce coronary heart disease events but have not been shown to reduce death from any cause.

Its main outcome evidence is ACCORD-Lipid: 5,518 people with type 2 diabetes, all taking simvastatin, who received either fenofibrate or a **placebo** (a dummy tablet). Over a mean of 4.7 years, heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death occurred at 2.2% per year with fenofibrate versus 2.4% with placebo. That is about 8% lower in relative terms and, over the whole trial, 0.74 percentage points lower in absolute terms. The result was not **statistically significant**, which means chance can't reasonably be ruled out.

A **subgroup** (a slice of participants analysed separately) with high triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol did better. Subgroup results raise questions; they don't settle them. Lessons 8 and 10 return to this.

## What to watch

The SmPC's warnings cluster in five places: the liver, the muscles (the risk rises when a statin is added), the kidneys, the pancreas and the gallbladder. It asks for **transaminases** (liver enzymes measured in a blood test) every three months in the first year, and for **creatinine** (a waste product used to track kidney function) in the first three months, then both periodically.

It must not be used in liver impairment, severe kidney impairment, known gallbladder disease, pancreatitis (unless caused by very high triglycerides), after a light-sensitivity reaction to a fibrate or ketoprofen, or with a peanut or soy allergy. Lessons 11 and 12 cover each of these.

## What this module is, and isn't

It is a learning module, not prescribing advice. Every lesson is dated to the SmPC revision above. The module is refreshed every six months, or straight away if the SmPC changes or a **safety signal** (new evidence suggesting a possible side effect) appears.

Where the evidence is uncertain, the uncertainty is part of the lesson.

cards.back: A family of lipid-lowering medicines that act mainly on triglycerides. Fenofibrate is one; bezafibrate, ciprofibrate and gemfibrozil are others.
Summary of product characteristics: the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers. In this module it always wins on what is approved.

## A medicine that has to be switched on

Fenofibrate itself does very little. It is a **prodrug**, a medicine the body has to convert before it works. Enzymes called **esterases** split it quickly after it is swallowed and release **fenofibric acid**, the form that does the work. According to the EU product information for Cholib, unchanged fenofibrate isn't detected in the blood.

## The switch it flips

Fenofibric acid activates **PPARα** (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha), a receptor inside cells that acts as a switch for genes involved in handling fat.

Flipping that switch does two things to triglycerides. It turns up **lipoprotein lipase**, the enzyme that strips triglycerides out of fat-carrying particles in the blood. It also turns down apolipoprotein C-III, a protein on those particles that normally brakes that enzyme. The result is more stripping and less braking, so triglyceride-rich particles are cleared faster.

## Fat travels in packages

Fat doesn't dissolve in blood, so it travels inside **lipoproteins**, particles of fat wrapped in protein. Those wrapping proteins are the **apolipoproteins**, which is why apolipoprotein C-III appeared above.

The SmPC describes fenofibrate's effect on three lipoproteins. **VLDL** (very-low-density lipoprotein), the main carrier of triglycerides, goes down. LDL goes down and shifts away from small, dense particles, a pattern the SmPC links to higher cardiovascular risk. HDL goes up, because PPARα also increases production of the apolipoproteins HDL is built from.

## Beyond blood fats

The SmPC lists further effects. Uric acid, the substance behind gout, falls by about a quarter. **CRP** (C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation) falls. Two clotting-related measures also fall in people who start with high levels.

All of these are changes in **markers**, things measured in the blood. None of them is proof of fewer heart attacks. Holding onto that distinction is the most useful habit this module can give you.

## What happens in the body

Absorption rises when fenofibrate is taken with food, which is why the SmPC says to swallow the tablet whole with a meal. Blood levels peak 4–5 hours after a dose. More than 99% of fenofibric acid travels bound to **albumin**, the main protein in blood.

Its **half-life**, the time it takes for blood levels to fall by half, is about 20 hours. It leaves the body mainly in the urine, almost completely within six days. Dialysis doesn't remove it. The kidney route is why kidney function drives the dose rules in Lesson 6.

## Why this matters for combinations

Fenofibrate isn't processed by **CYP3A4**, the liver enzyme that handles simvastatin, and it doesn't block it. That closes off one route for drug interactions with that statin. It doesn't remove the muscle risk the SmPC flags when a fibrate and a statin are combined, which Lessons 9 and 12 cover.

The SmPC does note weak-to-moderate blocking of CYP2C9, another liver enzyme. Medicines handled by CYP2C9 where a small change in blood level matters need closer monitoring.

## Why 160 mg isn't less than 200 mg

Secalip Supra contains **micronised** fenofibrate, ground into very fine particles, and the SmPC describes its **bioavailability** (the share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream) as higher than older forms.

That's why the SmPC allows switching from a 200 mg Secalip capsule to the 160 mg tablet with no dose adjustment. With fenofibrate, the milligram number on the box doesn't tell you on its own what the body receives.

## Sources

1. **SmPC** — Secalip Supra 160 mg, AEMPS CIMA, MA no. 63.533, text revision December 2020. Sections 4.2, 4.5, 5.1, 5.2.
2. **EPAR** — Cholib (fenofibrate/simvastatin), EMA product information, section 4.5 (simvastatin and CYP3A4) and section 5.2 (unchanged fenofibrate not detected in plasma).

## A French molecule

Fenofibrate was developed by Groupe Fournier, a French company, and has been in use in France since 1975. It is chemically related to two older fibrates, clofibrate and gemfibrozil. In the EU it has been sold mainly as Lipanthyl.

It reached the US market as Tricor in 1998, marketed by Abbott under a 1997 licence from Fournier. At that point it was already available in 77 countries.

## One molecule, many forms

Much of fenofibrate's later life has been about formulation. The EU product information covers capsules of 67, 100, 200, 250 and 300 mg and tablets of 145 and 160 mg. These include standard, **micronised** and **prolonged-release** forms (the last releases the medicine slowly over the day), and a **nanoparticle** form with even smaller particles.

Secalip Supra 160 mg, the product this module is based on, was first authorised in Spain on 1 September 2000.

## The question caught up with it

Fibrates came into use before many of today's lipid-lowering medicines existed. The EMA framed its later review around that fact: the question became where fibrates fit now that alternatives were available.

In 2005 the EU's **PhVWP** (Pharmacovigilance Working Party, the expert group then responsible for EU safety reviews) looked at all fibrates, because evidence of long-term cardiovascular benefit was limited. It found no new safety issues. It concluded that fibrates still had a role but should not be **first-line**, meaning the first treatment tried.

## The referral

Several companies disputed that restriction. So on 20 October 2009 the UK regulator triggered an **Article 31 referral**, an EU-wide review of a medicine class on public-health grounds. It asked the **CHMP**, the EMA's main committee for human medicines, for an opinion.

The CHMP agreed with the working party. Fibrates remain an acceptable option for lowering lipids, but first-line use isn't justified. There were two exceptions: people who cannot take a statin, and people with very high triglycerides, where fibrates lower triglycerides more than statins do.

## Why fenofibrate kept a third indication

Fenofibrate came out of the review with something the other fibrates didn't get. Based on new data from ACCORD-Lipid, the CHMP accepted its use alongside a statin in some high-risk patients whose triglycerides and HDL cholesterol stayed poorly controlled. That recommendation is the third indication in the Secalip Supra SmPC today.

The ACCORD paragraph the review added to the label is also still there. It keeps three things together: the neutral overall result, the better result in the high-triglyceride, low-HDL subgroup, and a possible harmful effect in women that can't be ruled out.

## Two medicines in one tablet

The add-on-to-a-statin idea then became a single tablet. Two **fixed-dose combinations** (two medicines in one tablet) were authorised for the whole EU at once. Pravafenix (fenofibrate + pravastatin) was authorised on 14 April 2011, and Cholib (fenofibrate + simvastatin) on 26 August 2013. Both are licensed only for high-risk adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia whose LDL cholesterol is already controlled on the statin alone.

Because they went through the EU-wide route, both have an **EPAR** (European public assessment report, the EMA's published evaluation). Single-ingredient fenofibrate was approved country by country and has none.

## Same evidence, a different ending in the US

On 18 April 2016 the **FDA** (the US Food and Drug Administration) withdrew the approval of fenofibric acid delayed-release capsules (Trilipix) for use alongside a statin. It concluded that the combined outcome-trial evidence no longer showed that lowering triglycerides or raising HDL in statin-treated patients reduces cardiovascular events. The withdrawal concerned fenofibric acid capsules specifically.

The Secalip Supra SmPC, revised in 2020, still carries the statin add-on indication, and Cholib remains authorised in the EU. Both regulators had the same trial data in front of them and reached different conclusions.

## Sources

1. **SmPC** — Secalip Supra 160 mg, AEMPS CIMA, MA no. 63.533, text revision December 2020. Sections 4.1, 5.1, 9.
2. **EPAR-level** — EMA, Fibrates Article 31 referral (2010–11): referral overview, questions and answers, Annex III.
3. **EPAR** — Cholib, EMEA/H/C/002559 (authorised 26 August 2013); Pravafenix, EMEA/H/C/001243 (authorised 14 April 2011).
4. **Pharmacovigilance** — FAMHP (Belgium), EMA recommendation to limit fibrates to second-line, 28 October 2010.
5. **US (differences only)** — Federal Register 81(74):22612–13, 18 April 2016.
6. **Secondary, dates only** — Pharmacology Update: Fenofibrate, new antilipemic agent. Clinician.com, September 1998.

## One condition behind all three uses

Every use in the SmPC carries the same condition. Fenofibrate is an **adjunct**, something added on top, to diet and to other non-drug measures such as exercise and weight loss. Those measures continue during treatment.

The SmPC also asks for **secondary causes** to be dealt with first. These are conditions that raise blood fats in their own right: poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, an underactive thyroid, nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder in which protein leaks into the urine), blocked bile flow in the liver, and heavy drinking. Some medicines have the same effect, among them diuretics, beta-blockers, oestrogens, oral contraceptives, immunosuppressants and protease inhibitors.

## Use 1: very high triglycerides

The first indication is severe hypertriglyceridaemia, with or without low HDL cholesterol. It is the one use where fenofibrate can be the first medicine tried, because the EU review found fibrates lower triglycerides more than statins do.

The SmPC doesn't put a number on *severe*. The US label does: 500 mg/dL or more, which is roughly 5.6 **mmol/L** (the unit most European labs report in). That number is shown here only to mark the difference between the two labels. It isn't an EU rule.

## Use 2: when a statin isn't an option

The second indication is mixed hyperlipidaemia when a statin is **contraindicated**, meaning it must not be used for that patient, or when a statin isn't tolerated. In this case fenofibrate takes the place of the medicine that would normally come first.

## Use 3: on top of a statin

The third indication is mixed hyperlipidaemia in people at high cardiovascular risk, taken alongside a statin, when triglycerides and HDL cholesterol are still not adequately controlled.

Three conditions have to be true at the same time: high risk, a statin already being taken, and a lipid problem the statin hasn't fixed. This is the indication the 2009–2011 EU review granted to fenofibrate alone among the fibrates, based on ACCORD-Lipid.

## Notice what isn't there

Look at how each indication is written. All three are defined by blood-fat levels. None of them promises fewer heart attacks, strokes or deaths, and the SmPC says plainly that fibrates have not been shown to reduce death from any cause.

The label doesn't support first-line use for ordinary high cholesterol. It doesn't recommend use under 18 either, because there are no data in that age group. And it asks for the response to be checked with blood-lipid tests: if the response isn't adequate after several months, other or additional treatment should be considered.

## A narrower door in the US

The US label for Tricor, revised in June 2025, has two uses. One is severe hypertriglyceridaemia. The other is lowering LDL cholesterol in primary hyperlipidaemia when the recommended LDL-lowering treatment isn't possible. There is no add-on-to-a-statin indication.

The US label also states that fenofibrate did not reduce coronary heart disease events or deaths in two large **randomised** trials (trials in which participants are assigned to treatment by chance) in people with type 2 diabetes.

cards.back: Something added on top of other treatment. Every fenofibrate indication is an adjunct to diet and non-drug measures.

Conditions or medicines that raise blood fats in their own right, such as uncontrolled diabetes, an underactive thyroid or heavy drinking. The SmPC asks for these to be treated before fenofibrate is considered.
Must not be used for that patient. One fenofibrate indication applies when a statin is contraindicated or not tolerated.

questions.explanation: That is the third indication, which the EU review granted on the basis of ACCORD-Lipid. None of the indications is defined by outcomes such as death. First-line use for ordinary high cholesterol isn't supported, and use under 18 isn't recommended.

## The tablet this module is built on

Secalip Supra 160 mg is a white, oblong **film-coated tablet** (a tablet with a thin outer layer), engraved with '160' on one side. Each tablet contains 160 mg of micronised fenofibrate. Packs hold 10 to 100 tablets, and hospital packs hold 280 or 300. Not every pack size is necessarily on sale.

Two **excipients** (ingredients other than the active substance) matter for patients: lactose in the core, and soy lecithin in the coating. The tablets keep for three years below 30 °C, in the original pack to protect them from moisture.

## One product, several names

The **PIL** (patient information leaflet, the plain-language sheet in the box) lists the same product under other names in other countries: Lipanthyl 160 mg in France, Lipidil-Ter 160 mg in Germany and Supralip 160 mg in the UK.

In Spain the **MAH** (marketing authorisation holder, the company legally responsible for the product) is Lacer, S.A. The tablets are made in France. Its sister product, Secalip 145 mg, still carries the Fournier logo on the tablet.

## The Secalip family

Spain has four Secalip products: Secalip 145 mg tablets (nanoparticle fenofibrate, ground even finer than micronised), Secalip Supra 160 mg tablets, Secalip 200 mg capsules, and Secalip 250 mg prolonged-release capsules.

The labels treat the first three as interchangeable: the 145 mg nanoparticle tablet, the 160 mg micronised tablet and the 200 mg micronised capsule can be swapped for one another without changing the dose. The milligram figures differ because particle size changes how much of the dose the body absorbs.

## Worth knowing: labels copy each other

In its dosing section, the Secalip 250 mg SmPC says that patients on a 145 mg or 160 mg tablet can switch to a 200 mg micronised capsule. That sentence is about a different product, yet it sits inside the 250 mg label.

It's a small slip, but it's a useful reminder. Product information is written by people, and text sometimes carries over from a sister product. Read the section you're relying on rather than assuming it's right.

## Generics

Several companies sell **generics**, which are copies authorised because they match the original product. Spanish packs mark them with the letters EFG. They include 160 mg tablets and 200 mg capsules from companies such as Sun, Pensa and Teva.

## Combination products

Fenofibrate also comes paired with a statin in a single product:

- Cholib: fenofibrate 145 mg with simvastatin 20 or 40 mg, as tablets, authorised EU-wide.
- Pravafenix: pravastatin 40 mg with fenofibrate 160 mg, as capsules, authorised EU-wide.
- Rosuvastatin with fenofibrate: authorised nationally in Spain by several companies, including Tecnimede, Intas, Viatris and Althera, in strengths from 5/145 to 20/160 mg. Most are tablets. Statifenix 20/160 mg is a capsule that contains two tablets.

None of these combines fenofibrate with ezetimibe. Lesson 9 returns to that gap.

## Outside the EU

In the US, Tricor comes as 48 mg and 145 mg tablets. Fenofibric acid, the active form of the medicine, is also sold there as a separate product.

In Switzerland, fenofibrate is available as Lipanthyl 200 M and 267 M capsules from Viatris. There is no 160 mg tablet.

## The routine

The dose is one tablet a day, with a meal. Swallow it whole with a glass of water, and don't crush or chew it. The PIL explains in one line why the meal matters: the tablet doesn't work as well on an empty stomach. That matches the SmPC, which reports higher absorption when fenofibrate is taken with food.

Diet and exercise continue alongside the tablet. They are part of the indication, not a warm-up before it.

## Checking that it works

The SmPC asks for the response to be measured with blood-lipid tests. If the response isn't adequate after several months, other or additional treatment should be considered.

The PIL adds that treatment is long-term. Patients shouldn't stop unless their doctor tells them to, or unless the tablets make them feel unwell.

## A missed dose

If a dose is missed, the PIL says to take the next one with the next meal and then carry on at the usual time. Never take a double dose to make up for a missed one.

## Kidneys: the rule this tablet can't follow

Kidney function is measured as **eGFR** (estimated glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter each minute, adjusted for body size). The SmPC sets three bands:

- Below 30: fenofibrate must not be used. If eGFR falls below 30 and stays there during treatment, stop it.
- 30 to 59: no more than 100 mg of standard or 67 mg of micronised fenofibrate a day.
- 60 and above: the usual dose.

Secalip Supra only comes as a 160 mg tablet, and it has to be swallowed whole. At an eGFR of 30–59, this product therefore can't meet its own label's dose limit. The PIL says the doctor may prescribe a lower dose, which would mean a different product.

## Kidney and liver checks

Creatinine should be measured during the first three months and periodically after that. Treatment should be interrupted if creatinine rises more than 50% above the **upper limit of normal** (ULN, the top of the laboratory's reference range).

Transaminases should be measured every three months for the first year, then periodically. Treatment stops if they rise above three times the ULN, or if hepatitis is confirmed. Fenofibrate isn't recommended in liver impairment at all, because there are no data.

## Special groups

People aged 65 and over take the usual dose, unless their eGFR is below 60. Under-18s: not recommended, as there are no data.

Pregnancy: use only after carefully weighing benefit against risk, because there are no human data. Breastfeeding: fenofibrate must not be used, because it isn't known whether it passes into breast milk.

## Overdose

Only isolated overdose cases have been reported, and most caused no symptoms. There is no antidote, and dialysis doesn't remove fenofibrate, so treatment is supportive. In Spain, the PIL directs people to the national toxicology information service.

questions.explanation: Between 30 and 59, the SmPC caps the dose at 100 mg of standard or 67 mg of micronised fenofibrate. Secalip Supra only exists as a whole 160 mg tablet. Fenofibrate is only contraindicated below 30, and the label doesn't mention alternate-day dosing.

## Sources

1. **SmPC** — Secalip Supra 160 mg, AEMPS CIMA, MA no. 63.533, text revision December 2020. Sections 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, 4.9, 5.2.
2. **PIL** — Secalip Supra 160 mg, revised December 2020. Section 3.
3. **US (differences only)** — Tricor (fenofibrate) prescribing information, June 2025 revision and earlier AbbVie version (strengths).

## Why this lesson comes first

The next two lessons are built from trials, and every trial appears on the same card so you can read each one the same way. This lesson covers the handful of ideas those cards depend on, using fenofibrate's own trials as the examples.

## Who gets what

A trial starts with a question and a group of volunteers. Before the real comparison, many trials use a **run-in**: a short lead-in period on a fixed treatment, to see who tolerates it and sticks with it. FIELD ran one on placebo and then one on fenofibrate, before anyone was randomised.

Randomisation comes next. In a **double-blind** trial, neither the participants nor the investigators know who is getting what, so expectations can't tilt the results. Trial registries sometimes call this 'masking'.

## What counts as the answer

Every trial names its **primary endpoint** in advance: the single measure that decides whether the trial succeeded. Everything else is secondary, and can only support or question that main answer.

Outcome trials often use a **composite endpoint**, which counts several kinds of event together. In ACCORD-Lipid it was the first occurrence of a heart attack, a stroke or cardiovascular death. Lipid trials use markers instead, such as the percentage change in triglycerides after 12 weeks. A marker tells you what the medicine did to the blood, not what it did for the patient.

## Two ways to state the same effect

In FIELD, 5.9% of people on placebo and 5.2% of people on fenofibrate had a coronary event over five years.

The **absolute risk reduction** is the plain difference between those two figures: 0.7 percentage points. The **relative risk reduction** expresses that difference as a share of the placebo figure, which the trial reported as about 11%. The same result sounds small one way and bigger the other. That's why this module always gives both, together with the comparator and the time point.

For lipid trials, the equivalent pair is each group's percentage change plus the difference between the groups, again with the comparator and the week it was measured.

## Hazard ratios and confidence intervals

Outcome trials usually report a **hazard ratio** (HR), which compares how often events happened in the treated group with how often they happened in the comparison group over the course of the trial. An HR of 0.89 means events happened about 11% less often.

The **confidence interval** (CI) is the range of values the data are compatible with. FIELD's was 0.75 to 1.05. That range includes 1.0, which means no difference, so the result wasn't statistically significant. The **p-value**, 0.16 in FIELD, says the same thing another way; the conventional bar is 0.05.

## Turning a result into people

The **number needed to treat** (NNT) is 100 divided by the absolute risk reduction in percentage points. It tells you how many people would need treating, for that length of time, to prevent one event.

In FIELD, total cardiovascular events, a secondary outcome, fell from 13.9% to 12.5% over five years. That's a 1.4-point difference, which gives an NNT of about 71 over five years. The trial didn't report this figure; it's calculated here from its numbers.

An NNT only means something when the difference is real. FIELD's primary result wasn't significant, so an NNT for it would dress up noise as a number.

## Who is counted, and what else they took

Most outcome trials are analysed by **intention to treat**: everyone is counted in the group they were assigned to, whether or not they kept taking the tablets. This protects the comparison from bias, and it means the result reflects the treatment as people actually took it.

That matters when people start other treatment on their own during the trial, which is called **drop-in**. In FIELD, 17% of the placebo group and 8% of the fenofibrate group started another lipid medicine, mostly a statin. The investigators said this may have hidden a larger benefit. It's also why every trial in this module is tagged with what participants were already taking.

## Better, or not worse?

A **superiority** trial asks whether a treatment is better than its comparator. A **non-inferiority** trial asks whether it is not worse by more than a limit set in advance.

One of Cholib's pivotal studies needed both answers: better on triglycerides and HDL, and not worse on LDL. It met the first two goals and missed the third. Lesson 9 shows the numbers.

## Subgroups and interactions

A subgroup result deserves attention only when the trial also tests for an **interaction**, which asks whether the treatment effect really differs between subgroups or only appears to by chance.

In ACCORD-Lipid, the test for a difference between lipid subgroups gave p = 0.057, just above the usual bar. The test for a difference between men and women gave p = 0.01. This module treats both as questions, not answers.

## The combination tags

Each trial card carries exactly one tag describing what participants were already taking:

- 🔗 +STATIN: everyone was on a statin, and fenofibrate was added or compared on top of it
- 🔗 +STATIN+EZE: everyone was on a statin plus ezetimibe
- 🔗 +EZE: everyone was on ezetimibe, with no statin
- 🔗 FDC: both medicines were given in one tablet or capsule
- 🔗 MIXED: some participants were on background lipid treatment and some weren't
- STATIN-INTOLERANT: participants couldn't take a statin
- MONO: no background lipid treatment

**Ezetimibe** is a cholesterol medicine that reduces how much cholesterol the gut absorbs.

## Reading a card

Every card has the same eight lines: the registry number, who took part, background therapy, what the treatment was compared with, the main question, the headline result, what it means in plain words, and what's worth knowing.

A **registry number**, such as an NCT or ISRCTN code, points to the trial's public record, where its plan was written down before any results came in. Comparing that record with the published paper is one of the simplest checks you can make.

## What 'pivotal' means here

A **pivotal trial** is one a regulator relies on to reach its decision. The Secalip Supra SmPC doesn't describe the lipid studies behind fenofibrate's original authorisations. It cites two large outcome trials instead: ACCORD-Lipid in section 5.1, and FIELD in the side-effects section. Those two shaped today's wording, so they are the pivotal trials in this module.

A third, newer trial follows them. It sits outside the label but is worth knowing about.

### Trial card: FIELD
Tag: MONO

- Registry: ISRCTN64783481
- Who took part: 9,795 adults aged 50–75 with type 2 diabetes, not taking a statin at entry; 2,131 had previous cardiovascular disease
- Background therapy: no lipid-lowering treatment at entry (see drop-in below)
- Compared with: placebo, over about five years
- Main question: does micronised fenofibrate 200 mg a day reduce coronary events, meaning coronary death or a non-fatal heart attack?
- Headline result: coronary events occurred in 5.2% on fenofibrate vs 5.9% on placebo over five years; HR 0.89 (95% CI 0.75–1.05), p = 0.16. That's about 11% lower in relative terms and 0.7 percentage points lower in absolute terms. It wasn't statistically significant.
- In plain words: the main question came back 'not proven'. A secondary outcome, total cardiovascular events, was lower (12.5% vs 13.9%; HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.99), mostly because of fewer non-fatal heart attacks and fewer artery-opening procedures. Death from any cause was 7.3% vs 6.6% (p = 0.18).
- Worth knowing: 17% of the placebo group and 8% of the fenofibrate group started other lipid drugs, mostly statins, which may have hidden part of the effect. Fewer people on fenofibrate needed laser treatment for retinopathy (3.6% vs 5.2%). There was also more pancreatitis (0.8% vs 0.5%) and more pulmonary embolism (1.1% vs 0.7%) — the figures the SmPC quotes.

### Trial card: ACCORD-Lipid
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT00000620
- Who took part: 5,518 adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk
- Background therapy: open-label simvastatin for everyone
- Compared with: simvastatin plus placebo; mean follow-up 4.7 years
- Main question: does adding fenofibrate to simvastatin reduce heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death?
- Headline result: 2.2% per year with fenofibrate vs 2.4% per year with placebo; HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.79–1.08), p = 0.32. That's about 8% lower in relative terms and, over the whole trial, 0.74 percentage points lower in absolute terms. It wasn't statistically significant. Death from any cause was 1.5% vs 1.6% per year.
- In plain words: across the whole trial, adding fenofibrate to a statin didn't reduce cardiovascular events.
- Worth knowing: in the 941 people with high triglycerides and low HDL, events were 12.4% vs 17.3% (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49–0.97), but the interaction test gave p = 0.057. A separate test pointed to benefit in men and possible harm in women (p = 0.01). ACCORD-Lipid also ran inside a blood-sugar trial, a 2×2 **factorial design** that tests two questions in one set of participants.

## What the regulator did with these two

Neither trial answered its main question with a yes. Even so, the EU review kept fenofibrate available, moved it to second-line, and granted the add-on-to-a-statin indication on the strength of the ACCORD data. The label prints the favourable subgroup and the warning about women side by side.

In 2016 the US drew the opposite conclusion for fenofibric acid. Both readings are on the record, and this module doesn't choose between them.

### Trial card: LENS (outside the label)
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: NCT03439345
- Who took part: 1,151 adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and early retinopathy, recruited through Scotland's eye-screening programme
- Background therapy: usual care; the share of participants on statins isn't confirmed in this module's notes, so this tag is provisional
- Compared with: placebo; median follow-up 4.0 years
- Main question: does fenofibrate 145 mg (daily, or on alternate days in people with impaired kidney function) slow progression to referable retinopathy or the need for eye treatment?
- Headline result: 22.7% on fenofibrate vs 29.2% on placebo; HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.58–0.91), p = 0.006. That's about 27% lower in relative terms and 6.5 percentage points lower in absolute terms over four years.
- In plain words: in people with early diabetic eye disease, fenofibrate slowed progression. This is not an indication in the EU label.
- Worth knowing: there was no effect on sight, measured as visual acuity, or on quality of life. Average eGFR ran 7.9 lower on fenofibrate, consistent with the creatinine rises the SmPC describes. Alternate-day dosing was the trial's own scheme and doesn't appear in the label.

## Why this lesson matters

Fenofibrate is rarely the only lipid medicine a patient takes. This lesson shows which partner medicines each licence actually names, sets the SmPC's own interaction lines side by side, compares what is known for fenofibrate alone and in combination, and lists every combination trial found in the registers.

## What the EU licences actually name

- Secalip Supra: 'a statin', without naming which one, in high-risk mixed hyperlipidaemia when triglycerides and HDL stay uncontrolled.
- Cholib: simvastatin only, at 20 or 40 mg, when LDL is already controlled on that dose.
- Pravafenix: pravastatin 40 mg or another moderate-intensity statin regimen, when LDL is controlled. That second option was added later; the original wording named pravastatin 40 mg only.
- The Spanish rosuvastatin + fenofibrate products: rosuvastatin, as a replacement for the same doses taken as separate tablets.

None of the EU fenofibrate licences reviewed for this module names ezetimibe.

## The SmPC's interaction lines

**Statins.** Section 4.5 of the Secalip Supra SmPC says the risk of serious muscle toxicity rises when fenofibrate is combined with a statin (the SmPC calls statins HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) or with another fibrate. The combination should be used with caution, and patients should be watched closely for signs of muscle toxicity. Section 4.4 goes further: co-prescription should be reserved for severe dyslipidaemia with high cardiovascular risk, in patients with no history of muscle disease, and under strict monitoring.

**Ezetimibe.** The Secalip Supra SmPC has no ezetimibe line at all. The ezetimibe SmPC covers the pairing from its own side: fenofibrate raised ezetimibe levels about 1.5-fold, prescribers should be aware of a possible risk of gallstones, and if gallstones are suspected the gallbladder should be investigated and the combination stopped.

## How to read those three columns

Read each column on its own, not against the others. Each column draws on different trials, in different people, at different doses. The table shows what evidence exists; it doesn't show which approach works best. No trial has compared all three head-to-head.

### Trial card: Cholib study 0501
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT00349375 (EudraCT 2005-003270-14)
- Who took part: adults with mixed dyslipidaemia at cardiovascular risk whose lipids weren't controlled on simvastatin 20 mg
- Background therapy: a simvastatin 20 mg run-in; fenofibrate was given as a separate tablet (**co-administration**), not as the combination tablet
- Compared with: simvastatin 40 mg, i.e. doubling the statin; 12 weeks for the main question, 24 weeks in total
- Main question: is fenofibrate 145 mg plus simvastatin 20 mg better than simvastatin 40 mg on triglycerides and HDL, and not worse on LDL?
- Headline result: at 12 weeks (493 vs 505 people), triglycerides fell 28.2% vs 4.6% (a 26.5-point difference). HDL rose 7.3% vs 1.6% (5.8 points). LDL fell 5.6% vs 10.5%, a 4.8-point gap in favour of simvastatin 40 mg, so non-inferiority on LDL was not met.
- In plain words: adding fenofibrate did more for triglycerides and HDL than doubling the statin, while doubling the statin did more for LDL.
- Worth knowing: the Cholib SmPC reports the missed LDL goal openly. This is an uncertainty stated as content, not hidden.

### Trial card: Cholib study 0502
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN

- Registry: NCT00352183 (EudraCT 2006-005851-14; ANZCTR ACTRN012605000777695)
- Who took part: adults without diabetes, with mixed dyslipidaemia at cardiovascular risk, whose lipids weren't controlled on simvastatin 40 mg after a six-week run-in
- Background therapy: simvastatin 40 mg, with fenofibrate given as a separate tablet
- Compared with: simvastatin 40 mg plus placebo; 24 weeks
- Main question: at 12 weeks, is the combination better on triglycerides, LDL and HDL?
- Headline result: at 12 weeks (221 vs 219 people), triglycerides fell 27.2% vs 0.7% (a 28.2-point difference). HDL rose 5.8% vs fell 0.8% (6.5 points). LDL fell 6.3% vs 5.2% (a 1.2-point difference, p = 0.54, not significant). At 24 weeks, the LDL difference was 7.2 points (p = 0.005).
- In plain words: on top of simvastatin 40 mg, fenofibrate lowered triglycerides and raised HDL. An extra LDL effect only appeared at 24 weeks.
- Worth knowing: the ANZCTR record lists its primary outcomes 'at 6 months', while the SmPC describes the primary criterion at 12 weeks. The only publication found so far is a conference abstract. Separately, the Cholib SmPC reports that fenofibrate lowered exposure to simvastatin's active form by 21–42% in three pharmacokinetic studies.

### Trial card: Pravafenix pivotal study
Tag: 🔗 FDC

- Registry: not found in this search
- Who took part: 248 high-risk adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia, not at their LDL goal on pravastatin (LDL at least 100 mg/dL, triglycerides 150–400 mg/dL)
- Background therapy: pravastatin 40 mg
- Compared with: pravastatin 40 mg alone, double-blind; 12 weeks
- Main question: does the combination capsule lower **non-HDL cholesterol** (total cholesterol minus HDL, i.e. all the cholesterol in potentially artery-clogging particles) more than pravastatin alone?
- Headline result: non-HDL cholesterol fell 14.1% vs 6.1% (an 8-point difference, p = 0.002). LDL fell 11.7% vs 5.9%.
- In plain words: over 12 weeks, the combination capsule lowered non-HDL cholesterol more than pravastatin alone.
- Worth knowing: the trial enrolled people who were not at their LDL goal, but the licence is for people whose LDL is already controlled. That's a gap worth reading about in the EPAR. Adverse events were reported in 36.6% vs 32.0% of participants.

### Trial card: fenofibrate + ezetimibe
Tag: 🔗 +EZE

- Registry: not found in this search
- Who took part: 625 adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia, on no lipid-lowering drug at baseline
- Background therapy: none. The comparison of interest is ezetimibe added to fenofibrate.
- Compared with: fenofibrate 160 mg alone (plus placebo and ezetimibe-alone arms); 12 weeks, with a 48-week extension
- Main question: does adding ezetimibe to fenofibrate lower LDL more than fenofibrate alone?
- Headline result: LDL fell 20% with both medicines vs 6% with fenofibrate alone at 12 weeks (a 14-point difference, taken from the published table).
- In plain words: the two medicines together lowered LDL more than fenofibrate alone.
- Worth knowing: the results in this module currently come from the US ezetimibe label's table of this trial. They will be replaced with the journal publication's figures. Neither medicine's EU fenofibrate licence names this pairing.

### Trial card: ezetimibe/simvastatin + fenofibrate
Tag: 🔗 +STATIN+EZE

- Registry: NCT00093899
- Who took part: 611 adults aged 18–79 with mixed hyperlipidaemia and no coronary disease (type 2 diabetes allowed)
- Background therapy: none at entry. The comparison of interest is fenofibrate added to ezetimibe/simvastatin 10/20 mg.
- Compared with: ezetimibe/simvastatin alone (plus placebo and fenofibrate-alone arms); 12 weeks
- Main question: what does adding fenofibrate 160 mg to ezetimibe/simvastatin do to lipids, and is it safe?
- Headline result: a follow-up analysis found larger falls in the cholesterol carried by VLDL, IDL and LDL, and a rise in HDL, with the three medicines together. On most lipoprotein fractions, though, the effects were not additive. The primary LDL figures from the main paper haven't yet been extracted.
- In plain words: the triple combination changed lipid particles more than ezetimibe/simvastatin alone, over 12 weeks.
- Worth knowing: this is the only triple-combination trial found. It measured lipids only, over 12 weeks, and no EU fenofibrate licence names this combination.
